newsitem.title: UK: UK M0 monthly growth slowest for nine months.
newsitem.headline: UK M0 monthly growth slowest for nine months.

text.p: The UK's narrow money supply measure M0, published on Monday, grew by just 0.1 percent in July on a seasonally adjusted basis, the lowest level since September 1996.
Analysts had been expecting a rise of 0.4 percent.
The annual rise was 5.9 percent, down from a revised 6.2 percent in June, and below predictions of a 6.2 percent gain.
But the indicator is unlikely to influence the central bank's decision on interest rates later this week, analysts said.
"M0 is the well behaved money supply measure. It's not going to cause much concern," said NatWest Markets economist John O'Sullivan.
"M4 is much more of a problem it has a much better correlation with the growth of demand," he said.

The Bank of England's interest rate setting Monetary Policy Committee is due to meet on Wednesday and Thursday and, according to a Reuter poll is likely to signal the fourth quarter point UK interest rate rise in as many months. British official rates are now at 6.75 percent.

M0 comprises notes and coins in circulation including those in banks' and building societies' tills and bankers deposits with the Bank of England but analysts say that the measure offers a better guide to consumer spending patterns if bankers deposits are excluded.
On this basis, there are tentative signs of a weaker retail sales figure in July than the hefty 0.6 percent increase seen in June, according to HSBC Markets UK economist Jonathan Loynes.
Seasonally adjusted notes and coins in circulation rose by 0.2 percent in July, down from 0.8 percent in June, whilst the annual growth rate dipped to 5.6 percent from 6.1.
"These figures provide the first hint that high street spending softened a little in July after the windfall-induced surge in the previous month," Loynes said.
British consumers have received a 35 billion stg boost to their spending power from building society flotations, provoking fears the economy could be on its way to an unsustainable boom.

"But they (the M0 figures) are unlikely to hold too much sway with the members of the Monetary Policy Committee if they are intent on raising rates again this week in order to dampen down domestic demand," he added.
"The M0 figures offer a glimmer of hope that perhaps the windfall spending has run its course," said CIBC chief economist David Coleman. "But you can't make much of a judgement on one month's data.
Moreover despite this month's slowdown, M0 is still above the official zero to four percent monitoring range and has been so since May 1993.

The usefulness of M0 as an economic gauge decreased when British interest rates tumbled in the early 1990s in a bid to get the economy out of recession -- lower interest rates meant there was less of an incentive to keep money in bank accounts rather than in wallets.
Analysts say that there is a possibility that the reverse situation is coming into play now -- UK interest rates are rising so keeping money at banks is a more attractive proposition.
"Although the interest rate cycle turned in October, it's only recently that that has fed into retail rates," Coleman said.

Changes in the way Britons pay for goods also mean that M0 figures are difficult to interpret, given the greater emphasis on using credit and debit cards as well as the wide availability of cheap credit deals.

Economists believe that the role of monetary aggregates in monetary policy has increased because the central bank rather than the Chancellor of the Exchequer is now calling the shots -- Chancellor Gordon Brown handed over interest rate authority to the central bank in May.

They argue that it is important to look a range of monetary indicators to get a clear picture. "I think the truth lies somewhere between M0, which seems to be coming down and M4, which is at record highs," said Peter Spencer, professor of financial market economics at Birkbeck College.

M4, which measures notes and coins and sterling deposits at banks and building societies, grew by 11.7 percent in the year to June, the highest rate since December 1990, fuelling fears that consumer spending is out of control.
Spencer argues that M4 is being distorted upwards by heavy cash holdings by large institutions who have cut their holdings of equities in favour of the allure of cash and gilts.
He argues that overall the Bank of England should hold off from raising interest rates again this month to allow the impact of the recent rate rises to become more clear.
